c.tagline: Where Mediterranean blue meets ancient Carthage stone.

taxi.fareNote: Meter starts around 4.70 TND by day (7.05 TND 21:00-06:00, a 50% night surcharge); insist drivers use the meter. Airport taxis instead charge a fixed fare of roughly 30-35 TND to downtown.

emergency.note: 198 reaches Protection Civile (fire/rescue); response times can be slow outside central areas, tourist hotels can usually assist in English/French.

hood_landmark.Les Berges du Lac: Lac de Tunis, Les Berges du Lac 2

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing in the medina and along Ave Habib Bourguiba; caution at night

hood_desc: Tunis's UNESCO-listed old city of narrow souks, mosques and centuries-old townhouses; best for culture-focused travelers who want to be immersed in history and don't mind noise and tourist bustle.

The 19th-century colonial-era new town centered on Avenue Habib Bourguiba, with cafes, banks and the widest choice of budget-to-midrange hotels; suits first-timers who want a central, walkable base near transit.
A modern lakeside business district of glass towers, malls and international hotel chains; suits business travelers and those wanting quiet, contemporary comfort away from the old city crowds.

An iconic blue-and-white clifftop village overlooking the Gulf of Tunis, full of cafes and art galleries; suits couples and photographers wanting a boutique, laid-back coastal stay a short train ride from downtown.
An upscale beachfront resort district north of the city with 5-star hotels and calm sandy coves; suits travelers who want resort-style relaxation with easy taxi access into central Tunis.
lodging: Radisson Blu Hotel & Convention Center, Tunis

water.note: Sources conflict on safety; high mineral content can upset visitors' stomachs, so bottled water is the safer choice.

transit.pay: Buy paper tickets or cards at station kiosks/vending machines for the Métro léger and TGM before boarding; city buses are typically paid in small cash to the conductor or with a Transtu card. There is no unified rechargeable card covering all modes for tourists.
transit.hours: Métro léger and buses run roughly 05:00-24:00 with reduced late-night frequency; the TGM runs about 05:00-00:00. There is no true all-night service, so use taxis or Yassir after midnight.
transit.note: Together the light rail, TGM coastal train and bus network cover Greater Tunis including La Marsa, Sidi Bou Said and Carthage; services can be crowded and schedules loosely kept, so allow extra time.

ferry: CTN ferries to Marseille and Genoa from La Goulette/Rades port

transit.m: SNT public bus to city center (30-45 min)

tip.r: 10-15% at sit-down restaurants is standard since service staff rely on tips; round up for taxis; not expected at cafe counters, bars, or hotel front desks.

food.name: Couscous
food.desc: Tunisia's UNESCO-listed national dish: steamed semolina under a harissa-red marka broth with lamb, fish or vegetables and chickpeas.

places.name: Dar Slah
places.note: Daily changing menu built around classic couscous; family-run for three decades.

places.name: Dar El Jeld
places.note: 18th-century mansion with a lemon-tree courtyard; the grand version of Tunisian cooking.

food.name: Brik a l'oeuf
food.desc: Paper-thin malsouka pastry folded around a whole egg with tuna, capers and parsley, then fried; eat it fast before the yolk runs.

places.name: El Ali
places.note: Traditional plates and a rooftop terrace over the medina rooftops.

places.name: Medina street stalls
places.note: Fried to order at lunchtime near the souks; the cheapest and crispest brik in town.

food.name: Lablabi
food.desc: Working lunch in a bowl: torn stale bread drowned in garlicky cumin chickpea broth with harissa, olive oil, capers and a poached egg.

places.name: Marche Central lablabi counters
places.note: Stand-up counters around the market serve it from mid-morning until it runs out.

places.name: Medina lablabi shops
places.note: Tiny hole-in-the-wall rooms; say how much harissa you want before they build the bowl.

food.name: Ojja merguez
food.desc: Eggs poached in a fiery tomato, pepper and harissa sauce with spicy merguez sausage or prawns, served straight from the pan.

places.name: Fondouk El Attarine
places.note: Restored caravanserai courtyard with Ottoman arches and live music most evenings.

places.name: El Ali
places.note: Good ojja and salade mechouia; stay for coffee on the terrace afterwards.

food.name: Chapati and mlawi sandwiches
food.desc: Tunisian street sandwiches: puffy chapati or flaky griddled mlawi stuffed with tuna, egg, olives, harissa and preserved lemon.

places.name: Central Market street stalls
places.note: Lunchtime queues of office workers; point at what you want in the fillings tray.

places.name: Avenue Habib Bourguiba side streets
places.note: Sandwich windows open late; cheap, fast and reliably fresh.

food.name: Grilled fish and bambalouni
food.desc: Mediterranean dorade grilled whole with lemon and tabil, and bambalouni, the sugar-dusted Tunisian doughnut fried on the seafront.

places.name: Chez Slah
places.note: Long-standing seafood institution; grilled dorade and seafood pasta are the picks.

places.name: Sidi Bou Said bambalouni stall
places.note: The stall by the steps has fried them for decades; eat them hot, standing up.

food.name: Mint tea with pine nuts
food.desc: Sweet green tea steeped with mint and floated with toasted pine nuts or almonds, drunk slowly in tiled courtyards and clifftop cafes.

places.name: Cafe M'rabet
places.note: Ottoman-era cafe with carpeted benches and columns; sit cross-legged for oud music.

places.name: Cafe des Nattes
places.note: The famous blue-and-white terrace cafe at the top of the village steps.

food.name: Celtia lager
food.desc: Tunisia's own pale lager, brewed since the 1950s and served cold in licensed restaurants, hotel bars and seafront terraces.

places.name: Le Golfe
places.note: Licensed seafront fish restaurant; cold Celtia with grilled catch and harissa.

places.name: La Marsa and Gammarth beach terraces
places.note: Licensed coastal terraces where a beer with dinner is entirely normal.

landmarks: Medina of Tunis
A UNESCO World Heritage old town of labyrinthine souks, mosques, and centuries-old mansions dating back to the 7th century.
Al-Zaytuna Mosque
One of the oldest and most important mosques in North Africa, its minaret rising iconically above the Medina's rooftops.
Bardo National Museum
A former Ottoman palace housing one of the world's finest collections of Roman mosaics.
Sidi Bou Said
A dazzling clifftop village of blue-and-white houses overlooking the Mediterranean, beloved by painters and photographers alike.
Carthage Ruins
The evocative remains of the ancient Phoenician and Roman city, including the famed Antonine Baths overlooking the sea.
Avenue Habib Bourguiba
Tunis's grand tree-lined boulevard, often called the 'Tunisian Champs-Élysées,' flanked by colonial-era cafés and landmarks.
Cathedral of St. Vincent de Paul
A striking neo-Romanesque and Moorish-influenced cathedral facing the sea at the entrance to Tunis's colonial district.
Antonine Baths of Carthage
The towering ruins of one of the largest Roman bath complexes ever built, set dramatically beside the Mediterranean coast.
Dar Hussein / Tourbet El Bey
Ornate historic mansions and mausoleums in the Medina showcasing exquisite Andalusian-Tunisian tilework and architecture.
Lake of Tunis and La Goulette
The scenic lagoon and port town gateway to Tunis, known for fresh seafood, colorful houses, and views toward the capital.

train.note: The cross-border Tunis-Annaba train (run jointly by Tunisia's SNCFT and Algeria's SNTF) reopened in August 2024 after about 30 years; it is a daytime service, roughly three departures a week from Tunis in the morning, taking about 9-10 hours via Ghardimaou, so bring your passport and confirm the current timetable. Domestic trains use Tunis-Ville station in the centre.

intl.op: cross-border coaches and shared louages — arranged locally at the terminals, no online booking

bus.note: Tunisia's national coach operator SNTRI (www.sntri.com.tn) runs long-distance buses within the country from Tunis; shared 'louage' minibuses cover most towns. Cross-border coaches and louages do run toward Libya (Tripoli) and Algeria, but they are not reliably bookable online - arrange them locally and carry your passport.

ferry.note: Ferries leave from La Goulette, the port about 12km north-east of central Tunis. CTN (which shares the Marseille route with Corsica Linea) and GNV/Grimaldi sail year-round to France and Italy, with far more sailings in the July-August peak, so book well ahead in summer and bring your passport plus vehicle documents if driving.

half.name: Dougga
half.blurb: Remarkably preserved Roman city set among rolling hills, with temples, theatre and mosaics.

half.name: Kairouan
half.blurb: Sacred Islamic city famed for its Great Mosque, walled medina and centuries-old carpet workshops.

half.name: Hammamet
half.blurb: Popular seaside resort town with sandy beaches, a whitewashed medina and citrus-scented gardens.

full.name: El Jem
full.blurb: Colossal Roman amphitheatre, among the best-preserved anywhere, rising dramatically above a small town.
